original_interpretation: TrendForce: Micron 23.3% of DRAM industry revenue in 2Q26.
evidence_found: "Micron continued to prioritize higher-priced server DRAM in its product mix amid capacity constraints. Revenue rose 65.5% QoQ to $36.0 billion in 2Q26, lifting its market share slightly to 23.3%." (TrendForce press release, 7 Sep 2026)
notes: Revenue-based TrendForce estimate (claim_type estimate is right). Industry total 'nearly US$154.73 billion'. Counterpoint puts Micron at 24% for the same quarter (CLM-1261); contradiction record added, comparable, method differences.

original_interpretation: TrendForce (Feb 2022): Ukraine supplied nearly 70% of world neon gas capacity.
evidence_found: "Ukraine is a major supplier of raw material gases for semiconductors including neon, argon, krypton, and xenon, according to TrendForce's investigations. Ukraine supplies nearly 70% of the world's neon gas capacity." (TrendForce, 15 Feb 2022, para 1)
notes: Accurately attributed as of Feb 2022 (historical). Not a current share: Ukrainian purifiers Cryoin and Ingas stopped production in March 2022 (USITC, SRC-0211), and USITC says Ukraine lost about 20% of global share after 2014. Treat as pre-war historical.

original_interpretation: Neon is part of the excimer gas mixture that generates DUV lithography light.
evidence_found: "In manufacturing semiconductor chips, a mixture of gases (termed excimer gas) generates the single wavelength of light used for deep ultraviolet photolithography. Within the gas mixture, neon is typically a buffer and carrier gas..." (USITC EBOT, Apr 2022, p.1 'Neon Market'); fn 3: ArF (193 nm) or KrF (248 nm).
notes: Neon is the buffer/carrier gas in the mix, not the lasing gas itself (ArF/KrF).

original_interpretation: USITC (Apr 2022): Ukraine supplied about half of world neon and was a major source of ultra-high-purity chip neon.
evidence_found: "Ukraine supplies approximately half of the world's neon and is a major source of the ultra-high-purity neon used in chip manufacturing." (USITC EBOT, Apr 2022, p.1 'Ukraine'); summary: "As of 2022, Ukraine supplies an estimated 50 percent of neon worldwide".
notes: Historical (as of early 2022). Production halted in March 2022 per the same brief. The EBOT carries a disclaimer that it is the authors' view, not the Commission's; better attributed as 'USITC staff briefing'. Same brief: Ukraine supplied about 70% of neon to chipmakers in 2014, which helps explain the TrendForce 70% figure (CON-0011).

original_interpretation: Neon comes from ASUs historically co-located with steel plants and is purified by specialist firms; Cryoin and Ingas halted by 11 Mar 2022.
evidence_found: "Large ASUs have historically been co-located with steel manufacturing, as the basic oxygen steelmaking process requires a high volume of pure oxygen..."; "As of March 11, 2022, Cryoin and Ingas, have been unable to continue production." (USITC EBOT, p.1)
notes: Compound claim (two facts); both supported. 'Specialised purification firms' is supported by the brief calling Cryoin/Iceblick 'gas purifiers'.

original_interpretation: Synopsys describes its business as spanning EDA software and silicon IP.
evidence_found: FY2024 10-K Item 1: "Synopsys, Inc. ... delivers trusted and comprehensive silicon to systems design solutions, from electronic design automation (EDA), including system verification and validation solutions, to silicon intellectual property (IP)." FY2025 10-K: "We deliver trusted and comprehensive solutions spanning silicon design, silicon intellectual property (IP), simulation and analysis (S&A) as well as design services."
correction: The FY2025 10-K (FYE 31 Oct 2025, filed Dec 2025) adds simulation and analysis (from the Ansys merger) and design services to EDA and IP. New claim supersedes this one.
notes: Correct for the FY2024 10-K.

original_interpretation: Synopsys names Cadence and Siemens EDA as its EDA competitors.
evidence_found: FY2024 10-K: "Our competitors include EDA vendors that offer varying ranges of products and services, such as Cadence Design Systems, Inc. and Siemens EDA." FY2025 10-K Competition section: "We compete with a variety of different EDA vendors, including publicly traded companies..." (no names).
correction: True of the FY2024 10-K only; the FY2025 10-K no longer names EDA competitors. Claim should be dated (new claim supersedes it).
notes: Cadence and Siemens EDA are still the main EDA peers per other sources (e.g. CLM-1468 foundry EDA partner lists), but Synopsys no longer says so in its latest 10-K.

original_interpretation: Synopsys's EDA and IP customers are mainly semiconductor and electronics systems companies.
evidence_found: FY2024 10-K: "Our Design Automation and Design IP segment customers are primarily semiconductor and electronics systems companies." FY2025 10-K: "Our EDA and Design IP customers are primarily semiconductor and electronics systems companies."
notes: Still holds in the FY2025 10-K. Note the FY2025 10-K adds S&A customers in a broad range of other industries; the claim is about EDA/IP only.

original_interpretation: Arm Q4 FY2026 licensing revenue USD 819m, royalty USD 671m.
evidence_found: "Licensing revenue grew 29% year-over-year to $819 million, driven by strong demand for the Arm platform. Royalty revenue grew 11% to $671 million..." (Arm Q4 FYE26 shareholder letter, 6-K Ex. 99.2, p.1); same figures in the 6 May 2026 call (Haas, 0:01:45).
notes: Arm IR transcript PDF (SRC-0213) only partly readable (CDN 403 to curl/browser; web_extract returned excerpts without these lines), so I checked against the SEC-filed shareholder letter, now added as a source. Quarter ended 31 Mar 2026. Population: 'license and other revenue' (CFO wording) includes US$200m from SoftBank-related agreements.

original_interpretation: Arm: customers can take Arm compute as IP, CSS or silicon; first production chip revenue expected in fiscal Q4.
evidence_found: Haas: "The Arm AGI CPU expands how customers can work with Arm. Customers can now deploy Arm compute through IP, compute subsystems, or silicon." Child: "we still expect the first revenues from production shipped sales to land in the fourth quarter of this fiscal year." (Q4 FY26 call, 6 May 2026, Yahoo/Quartr transcript 0:03:33, 0:12:11); letter: "Customers can consume the Arm compute platform using IP, CSS and now silicon".
correction: 'Fiscal Q4' means Q4 of fiscal 2027 (quarter ending March 2027), not the quarter just reported. July 2026 update: initial AGI CPU product delivered to multiple customers (new claims added).
notes: First sentence confirmed against the SEC-filed shareholder letter. Second sentence confirmed via third-party transcripts (Yahoo/Quartr; Morningstar snippet reads 'production chip sales'), because the Arm IR PDF could not be read in full. Forward-looking guidance, correctly typed reported_claim.

original_interpretation: Arm reports hyperscalers design custom chips: AWS Graviton/Trainium/Nitro, Google Axion, Microsoft Cobalt.
evidence_found: Letter: "AWS recently reported that their custom silicon business, including Arm-based Graviton alongside Trainium and Nitro, is now running at more than $20 billion annually"; "Microsoft continues to advance its Arm-based strategy with Cobalt CPUs"; Google TPU8t/TPU8i "will replace x86 host processors with custom Arm-based Axion CPUs" (Q4 FYE26 shareholder letter). Call 0:06:40 has the quoted wording.
notes: Arm's own account of customers (reported_claim is right). Trainium and Nitro are AWS custom chips but are not necessarily Arm-based CPUs; Arm says Graviton is Arm-based 'alongside' them.

original_interpretation: ASE describes itself as the leading assembly and test provider, also offering materials and EMS through USI.
evidence_found: "ASEH is the leading provider of semiconductor manufacturing services in assembly and test. The Company develops and offers complete turnkey solutions covering front-end engineering test, wafer probing and final test, as well as packaging, materials and electronic manufacturing services through USI" (6-K, 5 Feb 2026, 'About ASE Technology Holding')
notes: Self-description; 'leading' is ASE's own wording (reported_claim correct).

original_interpretation: EMS ~40% of ASE 2025 net revenue (NT$257.2bn of NT$645.4bn); packaging 48%, testing 11%.
evidence_found: "Net revenues from packaging operations, testing operations, EMS operations and others represented approximately 48%, 11%, 40% and 1% of total net revenues for the year"; table FY2025: Packaging 308,343; Testing 71,900; EMS 257,193; Others 7,952; Total 645,388 (NT$ million) (6-K, 5 Feb 2026)
notes: Unaudited. Computed EMS share 39.85%. Note EMS share fell from about 45.6% in 2024 (271,293 of 595,410), so the share is declining.

original_interpretation: Avnet describes itself as a global component distributor between manufacturers and customers, with design support, supply chain, programming, logistics and post-sales services.
evidence_found: "Avnet ... is a leading global electronic component technology distributor and solutions provider"; "works with electronic component manufacturers (suppliers) in every major electronic component segment to serve customers in more than 140 countries"; EC "offers ... turnkey and customized design, supply chain, programming, logistics, and post-sales services" (FY2026 10-K, Item 1)
notes: The services list is in the Electronic Components (EC) operating-group description, not the company-wide intro; minor scope point.

original_interpretation: Semiconductors ~79% of Avnet FY2026 sales of ~USD 27.6bn.
evidence_found: "During fiscal 2026, 2025, and 2024, sales of semiconductors represented approximately 79%, 78%, and 80% of the Company's consolidated sales, respectively"; table: Semiconductors $21,711.0m; Sales $27,632.7m (FY2026 10-K, Item 1/1A)

original_interpretation: Avnet supplier contracts generally terminable at will by either party.
evidence_found: "The Company's contracts with its suppliers vary in duration and are generally terminable by either party at will and upon notice." (FY2026 10-K, Item 1A Risk Factors)
notes: Located in Risk Factors, not Item 1 as the evidence said; also 'upon notice'.

original_interpretation: Chipmakers run captive mask shops but most keep relationships with merchant mask makers.
evidence_found: FY2021 10-K: "Nevertheless, most captive manufacturers maintain business and technology relationships with independent photomask manufacturers for ongoing support." Same sentence in FY2025 10-K, which adds: "there has been a tendency of more production being directed to the independent merchant manufacturers".
notes: Still current in the FY2025 10-K. FY2021 noted captive shops investing faster at the leading edge; FY2025 says share is moving toward independents. Typed reported_claim (Photronics' view), which is fine.

original_interpretation: Photronics named DNP, Hoya, LG Innotek and Compugraphics among merchant mask competitors (FY2021).
evidence_found: FY2021 10-K: "Our competitors include Compugraphics International, Ltd., Dai Nippon Printing Co., Ltd (outside of Taiwan and China), Hoya Corporation, LG Innotek Co., Ltd., Shenzhen New Way ..., Taiwan Mask Corporation, and Toppan Electronics Products Co., Ltd." FY2025 10-K lists the same four, with 'Tekscend Photomask' in place of Toppan.
notes: Accurate and dated FY2021. The four named firms are still listed in the FY2025 10-K. The full list is longer (Shenzhen Newway, Shenzhen Qingyi, SK-Electronics, Taiwan Mask, Toppan/Tekscend).

original_interpretation: Photomasks are custom products built from confidential customer designs.
evidence_found: FY2021 10-K: "Photomasks are manufactured incorporating circuit designs provided to us on a confidential basis by our customers." FY2025 10-K: "The photomasks we manufacture incorporate circuit designs provided to us on a confidential basis by our customers."
notes: Near-duplicate of CLM-1458 (FY2025 10-K).

original_interpretation: Test systems do wafer, package and system-level test; sold to IDMs, fabless, foundries and OSATs.
evidence_found: "The test systems we provide are used for wafer level, device package testing, and system level testing of semiconductor devices."; "Semiconductor Test products and services are sold to integrated device manufacturers ("IDMs")..., "Fabless" companies..., "Foundries"... and semiconductor assembly and test providers ("OSATs")" (Teradyne FY2024 10-K, Item 1)
notes: Same wording in the FY2025 10-K (filed 19 Feb 2026), added as a source. Teradyne's description of its own test market.

original_interpretation: Teradyne names Advantest, SPEA and Cohu among semiconductor test competitors.
evidence_found: "Competitors in the Semiconductor Test segment include, among others, Advantest Corporation, SPEA S.p.A., and Cohu, Inc." (FY2024 10-K, Item 1 Competition; identical in FY2025 10-K)
notes: Still current in the FY2025 10-K.

original_interpretation: AMAT AGS provides services, spares and factory automation software; a post-sale business distinct from new equipment sales.
evidence_found: "Our AGS segment provides services, spares and factory automation software to customer fabrication plants globally. Through October 26, 2025, our AGS segment also manufactured and sold 200 millimeter (200mm) and other equipment to customers globally that serve non-leading-edge markets." (FY2025 10-K, Item 1)
correction: In FY2025 AGS also sold 200mm and other equipment, so it was not purely post-sale. That business moves to Semiconductor Systems from Q1 FY2026.
notes: Opened via web_extract (the IR PDF blocks curl/browser). 'Distinct from new equipment sales' is the researcher's reading.

original_interpretation: Two customers ~19% and 15% of AMAT FY2025 net revenue.
evidence_found: "During fiscal 2025, two customers accounted for approximately 19% and 15%, respectively, of our net revenue." (FY2025 10-K, Item 1 Marketing and Sales)
notes: Fiscal year ended 26 October 2025. Customers not named.

original_interpretation: GUC sells ASIC design services and turnkey manufacturing from spec to finished product.
evidence_found: "GLOBAL UNICHIP CORP. (GUC) is a market leader in advanced ASIC (application-specific integrated circuit) services. Our comprehensive design services include 'spec-in' and SoC ... integration, physical implementation, advanced packaging technologies, turn-key manufacturing..."; "Our turnkey service models including spec-in, RTL-in, GDSII-in and KGD-in all the way to the finished product." (About GUC page)
notes: Company self-description.

original_interpretation: TSMC holds 35% of GUC shares and is GUC's sole foundry supplier.
evidence_found: "Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSMC) is our single largest shareholder who holds 35% of the company's total shares. TSMC is also GUC's sole foundry supplier as well as the closest partner in advanced process and packaging technologies." (About GUC, 'TSMC Partnership', accessed 2026-10-01)
notes: Undated web page; 35% is GUC's rounded figure. TSMC's own filings would give the exact stake (not checked).

original_interpretation: AWS says it has invested years designing custom silicon: processors, ML chips, storage products.
evidence_found: "AWS has invested years designing custom silicon optimized for the cloud. ... Our innovations include processors, machine learning (ML) chips, and high-performance storage products." (AWS Silicon Innovation page)
notes: web_extract truncated the page; read in full with the browser.

original_interpretation: Open market of independent distributors, brokers and online exchanges resells chips from many sources with no assurance of authenticity.
evidence_found: "The open market includes independent distributors, brokers, and on-line component exchanges that obtain products from a wide range of suppliers." (Exec. Summary, PDF p.2 / printed p.1); "once components are out of the authorized channel there are no assurances that the component is legitimate or functional." (printed p.19)
notes: Dated: SIA Anti-Counterfeiting Task Force report, August 2013. An industry body's view, typed as fact; better attributed to SIA.

original_interpretation: SIA recommends buying only from the OCM or its authorized distributors.
evidence_found: "The key to winning the battle against counterfeit semiconductors is elegantly simple: Exclusively buy semiconductor products either directly from the Original Component Manufacturer (OCM) or directly from the OCM's Authorized Distributors/Resellers." (Section XV, printed p.24)
notes: August 2013 report.

original_interpretation: Fabs rely on thousands of upstream suppliers giving hundreds of chemical, gas and material inputs.
evidence_found: "The supply chain required to fabricate chips is a globally integrated, complex network of thousands of upstream suppliers that provide fabs with hundreds of chemical, gas, and material inputs, each with precise requirements and their own sophisticated supply chains." (SIA testimony, 4 Mar 2026, p.6)
notes: On p.6, not p.2 as recorded. SIA cites McKinsey (25 Mar 2025, fn 8) for it.

original_interpretation: US share of global fab capacity was 10% in 2022, down from 37% in 1990 (SIA, 2026).
evidence_found: "While the U.S. commanded 37 percent of global fabrication capacity in 1990, our share of global capacity declined to 10 percent by 2022." (SIA EPW testimony, 4 Mar 2026, p.1, fn 2). SIA/BCG 2024 report: "raise its share of global aggregate fab capacity from 10% today to 14% in 2032" (p.4); Exhibit 7 (p.15) 1990 US 37%, 200mm+ commercial capacity, 300mm-equivalent, SEMI data.
notes: Testimony fn 2 cites SIA/BCG April 2021 (that URL now 404s); confirmed against SIA/BCG 2024 'Emerging Resilience' (SRC-0342), added as a source. Population: 200mm+ commercial fab capacity, excludes <5k wspm fabs; methodology SEMI data + BCG analysis. No newer actual (post-2022) share found; 2032 projection is 14%.

original_interpretation: Top three DRAM makers held ~87.6% of 2Q26 DRAM revenue.
evidence_found: TrendForce 7 Sep 2026: Samsung "market share of 39.4%"; SK hynix "market share edged down to 24.9%"; Micron "market share slightly to 23.3%". 39.4+24.9+23.3 = 87.6. Revenues $60.98bn + $38.59bn + $36.0bn = $135.57bn of ~$154.73bn (87.6%).
notes: Arithmetic correct and inputs verified (CLM-0554, CLM-0555 verified; CLM-0556 verified here). TrendForce estimate. Counterpoint gives 38+25+24 = 87% for 'DRAM and HBM' (CLM-1260/1261).

original_interpretation: Role boundaries are blurring: Arm sells its own chips, ASE ~40% from EMS, cloud providers design own chips.
evidence_found: Inputs: Arm 'Customers can now deploy Arm compute through IP, compute subsystems, or silicon' (CLM-0501); Arm July 2026: 'Initial product has been delivered to multiple customers' (new claim); ASE EMS 40% of 2025 revenue (CLM-0535, verified); AWS custom silicon (CLM-0503, verified) and hyperscaler chips (CLM-0502, verified).
correction: Arm 'is starting to sell' chips: deliveries began by July 2026, but first production chip revenue is guided for the quarter ending March 2027. ASE's EMS share is falling (45.6% in 2024 to 39.9% in 2025), and EMS through USI is a long-standing ASE line, not a new blurring.
notes: Reasonable interpretation: the facts support it, with these caveats on timing and trend.

original_interpretation: ASML installed-base sales ~25% of 2025 total net sales (EUR 8.2bn of EUR 32.7bn).
evidence_found: Inputs: CLM-0219 (verified) Installed Base Management sales EUR 8,193m; CLM-0217 (verified) 2025 total net sales EUR 32.7bn. 8,193/32,667 = 25.1%.
correction: The ~25% is right, but 2025 is boosted: ASML says many NXE:3800E field upgrades moved 'a substantial portion of EUV system revenue' into installed-base revenue (CLM-0220). One-company figure for 2025; it does not show a general 'large revenue pool for equipment makers'.
notes: Inference from verified claims CLM-0217/0219/0220; the evidence's 'c_asml_ibm' key maps to CLM-0219 / CLM-0509. ASML source not re-opened; relies on earlier verified checks.
